data.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 16 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Discoid lupus erythematosus** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. What is discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE)?**
- Commonest form of chronic cutaneous lupus — scarring, photosensitive plaques with adherent scale, follicular plugging, atrophy and dyspigmentation, mostly on head and neck; women 20–40 y; ~5–10% (more if widespread) develop SLE

**Q2. Describe the lesion.**
- Well-defined red-violaceous plaques with adherent scale extending into dilated follicles; on lifting, scale shows keratotic spikes on its undersurface — carpet-tack (tin-tack) sign
- Evolution: centre becomes atrophic, scarred, depigmented with hyperpigmented active border (in dark skin), telangiectasia
- Sites: face (malar, nose, ears — concha and external ear canal very typical), scalp (scarring alopecia), lips, V of neck, arms; localised (above the neck) vs generalised (above and below the neck — higher SLE risk)

**Q3. Name the variants of chronic cutaneous lupus.**
- Hypertrophic/verrucous DLE (extensor arms — mimics SCC/keratoacanthoma), mucosal DLE (lips, oral — risk of SCC), lupus profundus/panniculitis (deep nodules → lipoatrophy; face, upper arms, buttocks), chilblain lupus (acral purple papules in cold), lupus tumidus (urticarial plaques without epidermal change, very photosensitive), LP–LE overlap, childhood DLE

**Q4. Differentiate DLE from LP (PYQ).**
- See LP case — key points: DLE has adherent scale with follicular plugging, atrophy, scarring, depigmentation, photodistribution, ears and scalp; LP has purple flat papules with Wickham's striae, flexures, no atrophy (except atrophic/LPP), hyperpigmentation; histology and DIF differ (lupus band vs fibrinogen/cytoid bodies)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Face: psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, rosacea, polymorphic light eruption, sarcoidosis (lupus pernio), lupus vulgaris (apple-jelly, no follicular plugs), tinea faciei, tuberculoid leprosy, actinic keratosis/SCC (hypertrophic), Jessner's lymphocytic infiltrate, lymphocytoma cutis
- Scalp: lichen planopilaris, folliculitis decalvans, morphoea (en coup de sabre), tinea capitis (kerion), pseudopelade of Brocq, alopecia areata

**Q6. Histopathology of DLE.**
- Hyperkeratosis with follicular plugging, epidermal atrophy, vacuolar interface dermatitis with Civatte bodies, thickened PAS-positive basement membrane, superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate (patchy, dense), dermal mucin, pigment incontinence; scarring alopecia with loss of sebaceous glands
- DIF: granular IgG/IgM/C3 at DEJ (lupus band) in ~70–90% of lesions >6 weeks old

**Q7. Investigations.**
- Biopsy + DIF; CBC, ESR, urinalysis (proteinuria/haematuria), renal function, ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Ro, C3/C4 to screen for SLE; repeat yearly in generalised DLE

**Q8. Management.**
- Strict photoprotection: broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF ≥30 (UVA+UVB) daily, hats, clothing; stop smoking (reduces HCQ efficacy)
- Topical: potent/super-potent steroids (clobetasol) on body/scalp, mid-potency on face; tacrolimus 0.1% ointment (face); intralesional triamcinolone 2.5–10 mg/ml for thick or scalp lesions
- Systemic first-line: hydroxychloroquine 200–400 mg/day (≤5 mg/kg) — response in 2–3 months; chloroquine (more retinal risk) or add quinacrine (no retinopathy) if poor response
- Second-line: methotrexate, mycophenolate, dapsone (bullous/profundus), acitretin/isotretinoin (hypertrophic), thalidomide/lenalidomide (refractory — neuropathy, teratogenicity), anifrolumab (newer), JAK inhibitors (experimental)
- Camouflage, scar revision when inactive; lip lesions — monitor for SCC

**Q9. What is antimalarial retinopathy and its screening?**
- Bull's-eye maculopathy from cumulative dose; risk factors: dose >5 mg/kg/day real weight (HCQ), >5 years use, kidney disease, tamoxifen, pre-existing maculopathy
- Baseline eye exam then annual screening after 5 years (earlier if risk factors) — SD-OCT and automated visual fields (10-2)

**Q10. Complications of DLE.**
- Permanent scarring, scarring alopecia, depigmentation (cosmetic disfigurement), SCC in long-standing scars (lips, ears, scalp), progression to SLE (~5–10%)

**Q11. Pathogenesis of DLE.**
- UV-induced keratinocyte apoptosis releases nuclear antigens → plasmacytoid dendritic cells produce type I IFN → CXCL9/10 recruit CXCR3+ cytotoxic T cells → interface dermatitis, follicular destruction, scarring; genetic factors (HLA), smoking worsens disease and reduces antimalarial response

**Q12. Dermoscopy of DLE.**
- Active: perifollicular whitish halo, follicular keratotic plugs (yellow-red dots), arborising/ linear vessels, white scales
- Late: white structureless scarring areas, loss of follicular openings, pigmentation (speckled brown/ blue-grey dots)
- Scalp DLE: large yellow dots with thin arborising vessels (red spider in yellow dot)

**Q13. Scalp DLE — features and management.**
- Scarring alopecia with erythematous scaly patches, follicular plugging, depigmentation; hair-pull positive at active edge; treat aggressively (intralesional triamcinolone, super-potent topical steroid, antimalarials) to save follicles

**Q14. What is hypertrophic (verrucous) DLE?**
- Thick hyperkeratotic warty plaques on extensor arms/ face — resembles SCC, keratoacanthoma, hypertrophic LP; histology shows interface changes with marked hyperkeratosis; responds to acitretin/ isotretinoin, intralesional steroids, thalidomide

**Q15. Antimalarial dosing and combination.**
- HCQ ≤5 mg/kg real body weight/day; chloroquine ≤2.3 mg/kg/day; never combine HCQ and chloroquine (retinal toxicity); add quinacrine 100 mg/day to either for refractory disease (quinacrine causes yellow skin, rarely aplastic anaemia, no retinopathy); response takes 6–12 weeks

**Q16. What is the prognosis for DLE progressing to SLE?**
- ~5% of localised DLE and ~15–20% of generalised DLE progress to SLE, usually mild; risk factors — generalised lesions, high ANA titre, leucopenia, anaemia, raised ESR, arthralgia, nail fold changes, anti-dsDNA

## Quick spotter facts
- Carpet-tack (tin-tack) sign — DLE
- Concha of ear involvement — classic DLE
- Lupus band on lesional DIF

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous lupus erythematosus). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
